headline: A maximum-severity identity bypass leads a day of confirmed exploitation
standfirst: Standfirst: Three confirmed-exploited stories dominate — Cisco's 10.0 ISE authentication bypass, Linux kernel flaws newly added to KEV, and a pre-auth RCE in a workflow platform — while a 23.6-million-record breach and two enterprise patches fill out the rest.
bodyMarkdown:
## Actively exploited

Start with the one that scored the maximum. CVE-2026-76460 in Cisco Identity Services Engine carries a 10.0 CVSS score, and the vector leaves nothing out: network-reachable, no privileges required, no user interaction, scope-changed, full impact across confidentiality, integrity and availability [[s14]]. The root cause is insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint — CWE-648, incorrect use of privileged APIs — meaning a crafted request bypasses authentication and reaches the device without ever satisfying the web management interface. It is in KEV, with a short federal remediation window attached. The supplied affected configurations span ISE 3.1.0 from base through patch 11, and 3.2.0 through patch 10. ISE is the component that decides who joins the network; an auth bypass there is a beachhead into identity infrastructure, not a single bad appliance. Two practical notes: internet exposure is usually accidental rather than deliberate (guest portals, remote-access portals, stale NAT rules), and an authentication bypass means your logs will show successful-looking access.

The three Linux kernel flaws added to KEV deserve attention for a different reason [[s12]]. The one detailed here, CVE-2025-39682, is a mishandling of zero-length records on the TLS receive path's rx_list, classified as CWE-754 — improper check for unusual or exceptional conditions. NVD scores it 7.1, and its vector is local rather than remote, which is exactly the sort of number people use to defer action. Don't. KEV membership is a statement about observed exploitation, and local-root primitives are the payload half of container escapes, privilege-escalation chains and post-intrusion persistence. The affected ranges are broad: kernels from 6.0 up to but excluding 6.1.149, 6.2 to before 6.6.103, 6.7 to before 6.12.44, and 6.13 to before 6.16.4, plus the 6.17 release candidates, with Debian 11.0 named as well. Your distribution will backport; your job is knowing which fleet kernels still sit inside those windows.

Then there is Orkes Conductor, where CVE-2026-58138 is reported exploited in the wild before authentication ever happens [[s9]]. Version 3.21.21 through anything before 3.30.2 is affected: an attacker submits an inline workflow definition containing malicious JavaScript or Python expressions to the workflow API endpoint, and the platform's unsandboxed GraalVM evaluators — configured with HostAccess.ALL or allowAllAccess(true) — execute it through INLINE, LAMBDA, DO_WHILE and SWITCH task types, reaching OS commands by reflection or direct subprocess call. Scores are 9.8 on CVSS 3.1 and 9.3 on CVSS 4.0, CWE-94. What makes this worse than the score is position: workflow engines hold integration credentials, service tokens and the keys to everything they orchestrate. Note also that it is not in KEV — a confirmed catalog miss alongside reported exploitation, which is the cleanest possible demonstration that catalog absence proves nothing.

## Breaches

One server-side flaw was enough at Gyazo, where 23.6 million user records were taken [[s19]]. There is no CVE or vendor advisory metadata to reason about here; the lesson is the ratio. A single defect in a server component, against an account base of that size, converts one unpatched machine into a consumer-scale breach with the attendant credential-reuse fallout across other services. Worth using as a planning question rather than a postmortem: if one server in your estate fell tomorrow, how many records would that represent?

## Vulnerabilities

SolarWinds has patched a hard-coded key in Access Rights Manager, CVE-2026-28326, rated 8.8 and rooted in CWE-321 [[s8]]. The description is blunt — a static key in a product that brokers privileged access — and everything from version 2026.2 backwards is affected. It is not in KEV, and the CVSS vector is adjacent-network rather than internet-wide, so exposure depends on who can reach the service. Both facts should temper urgency, not cancel it: privilege-management tooling is a deliberate target, and a static key cannot be rotated out of trouble.

WordPress shipped core patches for a chain its reporters call Click2Shell [[s18]]. The core flaw lets a crafted link, opened by an already-authenticated administrator, install a theme from the official WordPress.org directory without anyone pressing Install; chained, that reaches code execution. No CVE is supplied, so prioritise by exposure instead: the attack needs a logged-in admin to click, and its trust boundary is the interesting part — a trusted directory, a legitimate session, and a URL. Patch core on any site an administrator logs into.

## Industry

A joint law enforcement advisory attributes a sprawling campaign to North Korea's WaterPlum, which compromised at least 30,000 devices between December 2025 and July 2026 and moved more than $10.7 million in stolen cryptocurrency back to the country [[s3]]. The scale is the story: this is volume-driven criminal infrastructure funding a state, and the operational takeaway is that endpoint compromise in service of cryptocurrency theft is now a mass-market problem, not a targeted one.

## Research

Finally, a chain worth studying rather than fearing: researchers used Claude Opus 5 to link two flaws and take over the ChatGPT and Codex accounts of several OpenAI employees, then reach an internal code repository [[s6]]. It began with a bug in the software running OpenAI's public help forum and moved through a weakness in the login system — sanctioned research, disclosed as such. Two lessons. Model-assisted offensive work visibly compresses the effort needed to stitch minor defects into a full chain. And the seam was not the flagship product: it was community infrastructure and the identity layer bridging it to everything else.

selected.excerpt: The authentication bypass flaw CVE-2026-76460 impacts Cisco's Identity Services Engine (ISE) and received a maximum 10 out of 10 CVSS score.

kev.vulnerabilityName: Cisco Identity Services Engine Incorrect Use of Privileged APIs Vulnerability
kev.shortDescription: Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE) and Cisco ISE Passive Identity Connector (ISE-PIC) contain an incorrect use of privileged APIs vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to gain unauthorized access to the affected device by bypassing the web-based management interface.
kev.requiredAction: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines.

nvd.description:
A vulnerability in an API of Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE) could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to bypass authentication.

This vulnerability is due to insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request to an affected API endpoint. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to gain unauthorized access to the affected device by bypassing the web-based management interface.

selected.angle: Cisco ISE's maximum-severity authentication bypass is already in CISA's KEV catalog, putting internet-exposed identity infrastructure at immediate risk.

selected.title: CISA Flags Three Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities Exploited in the Wild
selected.excerpt: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added three security flaws impacting the Linux kernel to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2025-39682 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper check for unusual or exceptional conditions vulnerability in the TLS receive path

kev.vulnerabilityName: Linux Kernel Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions Vulnerability
kev.shortDescription: Linux Kernel contains an improper check for unusual or exceptional conditions vulnerability in the TLS receive path which allows a zero-length record retrieved from the rx_list to bypass the intended recvmsg() record-type handling, potentially causing subsequent TLS records to be processed using incorrect zero-copy and queuing assumptions. The impacted product(s) could be end-of-life (EoL) and/or end-of-service (EoS). Users are advised to discontinue use and/or transition to a supported version.
kev.requiredAction: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines.
kev.notes: This vulnerability affects an open-source component, third-party library, protocol, or proprietary implementation that could be used by different products. nvd.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tls: fix handling of zero-length records on the rx_list

Each recvmsg() call must process either
 - only contiguous DATA records (any number of them)
 - one non-DATA record

If the next record has different type than what has already been
processed we break out of the main processing loop. If the record
has already been decrypted (which may be the case for TLS 1.3 where
we don't know type until decryption) we queue the pending record
to the rx_list. Next recvmsg() will pick it up from there.

Queuing the skb to rx_list after zero-copy decrypt is not possible,
since in that case we decrypted directly to the user space buffer,
and we don't have an skb to queue (darg.skb points to the ciphertext
skb for access to metadata like length).

Only data records are allowed zero-copy, and we break the processing
loop after each non-data record. So we should never zero-copy and
then find out that the record type has changed. The corner case
we missed is when the initial record comes from rx_list, and it's
zero length.

selected.angle: CISA's addition of three Linux kernel flaws to KEV confirms active exploitation, making urgent patching a priority for affected distributions.
